title: Dynamic Programming: Climbing Stairs (Bottom-Up)
oneLiner: How many distinct ways to climb n stairs, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time? Build the answer bottom-up in an array instead of recursing top-down.
keyTakeaway: Reaching stair i only has two possibilities: arrive via a 1-step from stair i-1, or a 2-step from stair i-2 -- so ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2), the EXACT SAME recurrence as Fibonacci. This is BOTTOM-UP dynamic programming (tabulation): instead of recursing top-down from n and caching along the way, fill an array from the base cases UP to n directly -- no recursion, no call stack, no memo dictionary, just a loop.
explanation:
Climbing n stairs one or two steps at a time, how many distinct sequences of steps reach the top? Think about the LAST step taken to land on stair i: it was either a 1-step from stair i-1, or a 2-step from stair i-2 -- there's no other way to arrive. So the number of ways to reach stair i is the number of ways to reach i-1 PLUS the number of ways to reach i-2: ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2). That's the exact same recurrence as Fibonacci (see Recursion: Fibonacci and Dynamic Programming: Fibonacci with Memoization) wearing a different problem's clothes -- recognizing "this recurrence IS Fibonacci" is a genuinely useful pattern-matching skill once you've solved Fibonacci once.

This lesson solves it BOTTOM-UP instead of top-down: rather than starting at ways(n) and recursing down to base cases (with or without a memo cache), build an array dp where dp[i] holds ways(i), filling it in order from the base cases (dp[0] = 1, dp[1] = 1) up to dp[n] directly -- each new cell only needs the two cells immediately before it, already computed. This is called TABULATION, and it has a real advantage over the top-down memoized version: no recursion means no call stack at all, which matters for large n where deep recursion could hit a stack limit that a simple loop never would.

Watch the array fill left to right below -- each new cell's value is read directly off the two cells immediately behind it, exactly like the recurrence says.

complexity.note: One left-to-right fill of an n+1 array. Since each cell only reads the previous two, you can keep just two variables for O(1) space.

referenceSolutions.python:
def climb_stairs(n):
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    dp[0] = 1
    dp[1] = 1
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2]
    return dp[n]
